newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria can't shake off voided poll four years on.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria can't shake off voided poll four years on.

text.p: Four years after annulling a poll to restore civil rule, Nigeria is now heading efforts to bring back democracy to Sierra Leone even though the populous nation itself remains in turmoil over its failure to end military rule.

"That is the irony about Nigeria: a leading African nation seen as unwilling to restore democracy at home seeks the reinstatement of an elected president elsewhere," said a Western diplomat who has followed the crisis triggered when ruling generals scrapped a presidential election in 1993.
Nigeria is leading a regional force in Sierra Leone to reinstate President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, toppled by low-ranking soldiers on May 25 in a coup which drew worldwide condemnation.

"Charity, it is said, should begin at home. But Nigeria's charity is beginning abroad," said the opposition Tell magazine in an editorial on Monday in which it asked the Abuja government to restore democracy in Nigeria first.
Africa's most populous nation has been in turmoil since the 1993 election was scrapped.
Four days to the fourth anniversary of the annulled June 12, 1993 election, police are on alert for violence if opponents try to commemorate the scrapped elections.

"We have mapped out strategies to contain miscreants who may like to forment trouble. We shall deal ruthlessly with anybody caught," said police commissioner Ogbona Onovo of Ogun state, the home of Moshood Abiola, the incarcerated businessman presumed to have won the annulled vote.
"All political rallies and public meetings have been banned until after June 12," Onovo told reporters in the state capital Abeokuta at the weekend.
Local newspapers say thousands of police will be on the streets over the anniversary, even though the umbrella opposition group NADECO says it plans no public protests.

"If you judge progress just by demonstration, placard carrying, the leadership of NADECO has resolved that we are not going to do that because we know that the present regime would not hesitate to shoot and kill," said NADECO's acting chairman Abraham Adesanya.
Foreign-based opposition group Free Nigeria Movement faxed a statement to the media in Nigeria saying it would launch an anti-government radio station on June 12.
But otherwise it would appear as if fatigue has set in on the annual protests over "June 12", as the crisis unleashed by the scrapped election is now known.
Political sources say the main rallies this time will call on military ruler General Sani Abacha to contest next year's presidential election to become Nigeria's elected president.
Abacha is implementing his own programme to restore democracy in October next year although the opposition and the West doubt the generals are keen to let go of power.
Abacha has himself not said he will contest the presidential vote but several groups have emerged to press him to do so and there is no official indication they are unwelcome.
"I have no doubt in my mind that pro-Abacha groups would be allowed to organise their rallies but if pro-democracy groups attempt to do the same, they will be mowed down like grass," said Adesanya.
Abiola will mark three years in detention on June 23, the anniversary of his arrest in 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of the military rulers.
Nigeria's relations with its traditional Western partners have soured and taken a toll on the country's economy, which in turn has helped to impoverish its 104 million people.
